claim: Core gene phylogenies inferred from a small set of universal core genes have typically supported a long branch separating the archaeal and bacterial domains.
source: Trees inferred from a small set of universal core genes have typically supported a long branch separating the archaeal and bacterial domains.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies that have inferred such trees.

claim: Recent analyses of a broader set of non-ribosomal genes have suggested that Archaea may be less divergent from Bacteria.
source: By contrast, recent analyses of a broader set of non-ribosomal genes have suggested that Archaea may be less divergent from Bacteria, and that estimates of inter-domain distance are inflated due to accelerated evolution of ribosomal proteins along the inter-domain branch.
evidence: The claim references recent analyses that have made this suggestion.

claim: Estimates of inter-domain distance are inflated due to accelerated evolution of ribosomal proteins along the inter-domain branch.
source: By contrast, recent analyses of a broader set of non-ribosomal genes have suggested that Archaea may be less divergent from Bacteria, and that estimates of inter-domain distance are inflated due to accelerated evolution of ribosomal proteins along the inter-domain branch.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed in recent analyses.

claim: Estimates of a reduced Archaea-Bacteria (AB) branch length result from inter-domain gene transfers and hidden paralogy in the expanded marker gene set.
source: We show that estimates of a reduced Archaea-Bacteria (AB) branch length result from inter-domain gene transfers and hidden paralogy in the expanded marker gene set.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of the expanded marker gene set, including manual inspection of gene trees and statistical tests.

claim: Current methods likely underestimate the AB branch length due to substitutional saturation and poor model fit.
source: By contrast, analysis of a broad range of manually curated marker gene datasets from an evenly sampled set of 700 Archaea and Bacteria reveals that current methods likely underestimate the AB branch length due to substitutional saturation and poor model fit
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of marker gene datasets, including comparisons of different substitution models and site evolutionary rates.

claim: The best-performing phylogenetic markers tend to support longer inter-domain branch lengths.
source: that the best-performing phylogenetic markers tend to support longer inter-domain branch lengths
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' ranking of markers based on split scores and their correlation with AB branch length.

claim: The AB branch lengths of ribosomal and non-ribosomal marker genes are statistically indistinguishable.
source: and that the AB branch lengths of ribosomal and non-ribosomal marker genes are statistically indistinguishable.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of AB branch lengths from ribosomal and non-ribosomal marker gene concatenates.

claim: The phylogeny inferred from the 27 highest-ranked marker genes recovers a clade of DPANN at the base of the Archaea.
source: Furthermore, our phylogeny inferred from the 27 highest-ranked marker genes recovers a clade of DPANN at the base of the Archaea
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree inferred from the 27 marker genes.

claim: The phylogeny inferred from the 27 highest-ranked marker genes places the bacterial Candidate Phyla Radiation (CPR) within Bacteria as the sister group to the Chloroflexota.
source: and places the bacterial Candidate Phyla Radiation (CPR) within Bacteria as the sister group to the Chloroflexota.
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree inferred from the 27 marker genes.

claim: Universal core genes are thought to predominantly evolve vertically and are thus best suited for reconstructing the tree of life.
source: While representing a small fraction of the total genome of any organism (Dagan and Martin, 2006), these genes are thought to predominantly evolve vertically and are thus best suited for reconstructing the tree of life (Ciccarelli et al., 2006; Creevey et al., 2011; Puigbò et al., 2009; Ramulu et al., 2014; Theobald, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In analyses of universal core genes, the branch separating Archaea from Bacteria is often the longest internal branch in the tree.
source: In these analyses, the branch separating Archaea from Bacteria (hereafter, the AB branch) is often the longest internal branch in the tree (Cox et al., 2008; Gogarten et al., 1989; Hug et al., 2016; Iwabe et al., 1989; Pühler et al., 1989; Williams et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Long branches can result from high evolutionary rates, long periods of absolute time, or a combination of the two.
source: Long branches can therefore result from high evolutionary rates, long periods of absolute time, or a combination of the two.
evidence: The claim is based on established principles of molecular phylogenetics.

claim: Limited fossil data is currently available to calibrate early divergences in the tree of life.
source: However, limited fossil data (Sugitani et al., 2015) is currently available to calibrate early divergences in the tree of life (Betts et al., 2018; Horita and Berndt, 1999; Lepland et al., 2002; van Zuilen et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on fossil evidence and molecular clock calibration.

claim: The ages and evolutionary rates of the deepest branches of the tree remain highly uncertain.
source: and as a result, the ages and evolutionary rates of the deepest branches of the tree remain highly uncertain.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the limited availability of fossil calibrations.

claim: Zhu et al., 2019 inferred a phylogeny from 381 genes distributed across Archaea and Bacteria using the supertree method ASTRAL.
source: Recently, Zhu et al., 2019 inferred a phylogeny from 381 genes distributed across Archaea and Bacteria using the supertree method ASTRAL (Mirarab et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about a previous study.

claim: The 381 markers comprise not only proteins involved in information processing but also proteins affiliated with most other functional COG categories, including metabolic processes.
source: These markers increase the total number of genes compared to other universal marker sets and comprise not only proteins involved in information processing but also proteins affiliated with most other functional COG categories, including metabolic processes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' annotation of the 381 marker genes.

claim: The genetic distance (AB branch length) between the domains inferred by Zhu et al., 2019 was much shorter than observed with the core universal markers.
source: The genetic distance (AB branch length) between the domains (Zhu et al., 2019) was estimated from a concatenation of the same marker genes, resulting in a much shorter AB branch length than observed with the core universal markers (Hug et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is a comparison of results from different studies.

claim: The apparent deep divergence of Archaea and Bacteria might be the result of an accelerated evolutionary rate of genes encoding translational and in particular ribosomal proteins along the AB branch as compared to other genes.
source: These analyses were consistent with the hypothesis (Petitjean et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2019) that the apparent deep divergence of Archaea and Bacteria might be the result of an accelerated evolutionary rate of genes encoding translational and in particular ribosomal proteins along the AB branch as compared to other genes.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed in previous studies.

claim: A higher evolutionary rate of ribosomal genes might result from the accumulation of compensatory substitutions at the interaction surfaces among the protein subunits of the ribosome.
source: A higher evolutionary rate of ribosomal genes might result from the accumulation of compensatory substitutions at the interaction surfaces among the protein subunits of the ribosome (Petitjean et al., 2014; Valas and Bourne, 2011)
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed in previous studies.

claim: A higher evolutionary rate of ribosomal genes might result as a compensatory response to the addition or removal of ribosomal subunits early in evolution.
source: or as a compensatory response to the addition or removal of ribosomal subunits early in evolution (Petitjean et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed in a previous study.

claim: Substitutional saturation and across-site compositional heterogeneity can both impact the inference of tree topologies and branch lengths.
source: Substitutional saturation (multiple substitutions at the same site) (Jeffroy et al., 2006) and across-site compositional heterogeneity can both impact the inference of tree topologies and branch lengths (Foster, 2004; Lartillot et al., 2007; Lartillot and Philippe, 2004; Quang et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008; Williams et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on phylogenetic methods.

claim: These difficulties are particularly significant for ancient divergences.
source: These difficulties are particularly significant for ancient divergences (Gouy et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Failure to model site-specific amino acid preferences has previously been shown to lead to underestimation of the AB branch length due to a failure to detect convergent changes.
source: Failure to model site-specific amino acid preferences has previously been shown to lead to underestimation of the AB branch length due to a failure to detect convergent changes (Tourasse and Gouy, 1999; Williams et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The published analysis of the 381 marker set did not find evidence of a substantial impact of substitutional saturation and compositional heterogeneity on the tree as a whole.
source: although the published analysis of the 381 marker set did not find evidence of a substantial impact of these features on the tree as a whole (Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is a statement about the findings of a previous study.

claim: The published analyses of the 381 marker set identified phylogenetic incongruence among the 381 markers, but did not determine the underlying cause.
source: Those analyses also identified phylogenetic incongruence among the 381 markers, but did not determine the underlying cause (Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is a statement about the findings of a previous study.

claim: 41% of the published gene trees from the expanded marker set contain less than 25% of the sampled archaea.
source: Specifically, 41% of the published gene trees (https://biocore.github.io/wol/; Zhu et al., 2019) contain less than 25% of the sampled archaea
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of the published gene trees.

claim: 14 of the published gene trees from the expanded marker set include 0 archaeal homologues.
source: with 14 and 68 of these trees including 0 or ≤10 archaeal homologues, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of the published gene trees.

claim: 68 of the published gene trees from the expanded marker set include ≤10 archaeal homologues.
source: with 14 and 68 of these trees including 0 or ≤10 archaeal homologues, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of the published gene trees.

claim: Across all of the gene trees in the expanded marker set, archaeal homologues comprise 0–14.8% of the dataset.
source: Across all of the gene trees, archaeal homologues comprise 0–14.8% of the dataset (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of the published gene trees.

claim: 317/381 gene trees from the expanded marker set did not possess an unambiguous branch separating the archaeal and bacterial domains.
source: Manual inspection of subsampled versions of these gene trees suggested that 317/381 did not possess an unambiguous branch separating the archaeal and bacterial domains (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' manual inspection of gene trees.

claim: Many of the 381 marker genes are not broadly present in both domains, and some might be specific to Bacteria.
source: These distributions suggest that many of these genes are not broadly present in both domains, and that some might be specific to Bacteria.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' analysis of gene tree distributions.

claim: In the published analysis of the 381-gene set, the tree topology was inferred using the supertree method ASTRAL, with branch lengths inferred on this fixed tree from a marker gene concatenation.
source: In the published analysis of the 381-gene set (Zhu et al., 2019), the tree topology was inferred using the supertree method ASTRAL (Mirarab et al., 2014), with branch lengths inferred on this fixed tree from a marker gene concatenation (Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is a description of the methods used in a previous study.

claim: The topology inferred from the expanded marker set is similar to previous trees and recovers Archaea and Bacteria as reciprocally monophyletic domains.
source: The topology inferred from this expanded marker set (Zhu et al., 2019) is similar to previous trees (Castelle and Banfield, 2018; Hug et al., 2016) and recovers Archaea and Bacteria as reciprocally monophyletic domains, albeit with a shorter AB branch than in earlier analyses.
evidence: The claim is a comparison of results from different studies.

claim: Archaea and Bacteria are recovered as reciprocally monophyletic groups in only 22 of the 381 published maximum likelihood gene trees of the expanded marker set.
source: However, the individual gene trees (Zhu et al., 2019) differ regarding domain monophyly: Archaea and Bacteria are recovered as reciprocally monophyletic groups in only 22 of the 381 published (Zhu et al., 2019) maximum likelihood (ML) gene trees of the expanded marker set (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of the published gene trees.

claim: Domain monophyly was rejected at the 5% significance level (with Bonferroni correction, p<0.0001656) for 151 out of 302 genes in the expanded marker set.
source: For the remaining 302 genes, domain monophyly was rejected at the 5% significance level (with Bonferroni correction, p<0.0001656) for 151 out of 302 (50%) genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' AU tests on the expanded marker set.

claim: None of the markers in the core, non-ribosomal, and bacterial sets rejected reciprocal domain monophyly.
source: As a comparison, we performed the same test on several smaller marker sets used previously to infer a tree of life (Coleman et al., 2021; Petitjean et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2020); none of the markers in those sets rejected reciprocal domain monophyly (p<0.05 for all genes, with Bonferroni correction: Coleman: >0.001724; Petitjean: >0.001316; Williams: >0.00102: Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' AU tests on other marker sets.

claim: Expanded set genes that reject domain monophyly support significantly shorter Archaea-Bacteria branch lengths when constrained to follow a domain monophyletic tree.
source: Expanded set genes that reject domain monophyly (p<0.05, approximately unbiased [AU] test, with Bonferroni correction [see main text]) support significantly shorter Archaea-Bacteria (AB) branch lengths when constrained to follow a domain monophyletic tree (p=3.653 × 10–6, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: AB branch length and relative AB distance are positively correlated (R = 0.7426499, p< 2.2 × 10–16).
source: (B) Two measures of evolutionary proximity (Zhu et al., 2019), AB branch length and relative AB distance, are positively correlated (R = 0.7426499, p< 2.2 × 10–16).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ∆LL is negatively correlated with AB branch length (p=0.009013 and R = –0.2317894).
source: We considered two complementary proxies of marker gene verticality: ∆LL (C: against AB branch length; D: against relative AB length), which reflects the degree to which marker genes reject domain monophyly (C: p=0.009013 and R = –0.2317894
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ∆LL is negatively correlated with relative AB length (p=0.0001051 and R = –0.2213292).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The between-domain split score is negatively correlated with AB branch length (p=0.0005304 and R = –0.3043537).
source: and the between-domain split score (E: against AB branch length; F: against relative AB length), which quantifies the extent to which marker genes recover monophyletic Archaea and Bacteria; a higher split score (see Materials and methods) indicates the splitting of domains into multiple gene tree clades due to gene transfer, reciprocal sorting out of paralogs, or lack of phylogenetic resolution (E: p=0.0005304 and R = –0.3043537
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The between-domain split score is negatively correlated with relative AB length (p=2.572 × 10–6 and R = –0.2667739).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Between- and within-domain split scores are positively correlated (R = 0.836679, p<2.2 × 10–16).
source: We also considered a split score based on within-domain relationships (G); between- and within-domain split scores are positively correlated: R = 0.836679, p<2.2 × 10–16, Pearson's correlation, indicating that markers that recover Archaea and Bacteria as monophyletic also tend to recover established within-domain relationships.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Markers that recover Archaea and Bacteria as monophyletic also tend to recover established within-domain relationships.
source: indicating that markers that recover Archaea and Bacteria as monophyletic also tend to recover established within-domain relationships.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the positive correlation between between- and within-domain split scores.

claim: Inferred AB length decreases as marker genes of lower verticality (larger ∆LL) are added to the concatenate.
source: (H) Inferred AB length decreases as marker genes of lower verticality (larger ∆LL) are added to the concatenate.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The major cause of domain polyphyly observed in gene trees was inter-domain gene transfer (in 359 out of 381 gene trees [94.2%]).
source: This revealed that the major cause of domain polyphyly observed in gene trees was inter-domain gene transfer (in 359 out of 381 gene trees [94.2%])
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' manual inspection of gene trees.

claim: Mixing of sequences from distinct paralogous families was observed in 246 out of 381 gene trees (64.6%).
source: and mixing of sequences from distinct paralogous families (in 246 out of 381 gene trees [64.6%]).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' manual inspection of gene trees.

claim: AB branch lengths were significantly shorter for markers that rejected domain monophyly (mean AB branch length was 0.00668 substitutions/site) compared to markers that did not reject domain monophyly (mean AB branch length was 0.287 substitutions/site).
source: AB branch lengths were significantly (p=3.653 × 10–6, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) shorter for markers that rejected domain monophyly (Bonferroni-corrected p<0.0001656; Figure 1A): the mean AB branch length was 0.00668 substitutions/site for markers that significantly rejected domain monophyly and 0.287 substitutions/site for markers that did not reject domain monophyly.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of AB branch lengths.

claim: Marker gene transfers reduce the number of fixed differences between the domains, so that the AB branch length in a tree in which Archaea and Bacteria are constrained to be reciprocally monophyletic will tend towards 0 as the number of transfers increases.
source: This behavior might result from marker gene transfers reducing the number of fixed differences between the domains, so that the AB branch length in a tree in which Archaea and Bacteria are constrained to be reciprocally monophyletic will tend towards 0 as the number of transfers increases.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain their observations.

claim: Genes that recover the reciprocal monophyly of Archaea and Bacteria also evolve more vertically within each domain.
source: Overall, these results suggest that genes that recover the reciprocal monophyly of Archaea and Bacteria also evolve more vertically within each domain
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the positive correlation between between- and within-domain split scores.

claim: Vertically evolving marker genes support a longer AB branch and a greater AB distance.
source: and that these vertically evolving marker genes support a longer AB branch and a greater AB distance.
evidence: The claim is supported by the negative correlations between split scores/∆LL and AB branch length/relative AB distance.

claim: AB branch lengths estimated using concatenation decreased as increasing numbers of low-verticality markers were added to the concatenate.
source: Consistent with these inferences, AB branch lengths estimated using concatenation decreased as increasing numbers of low-verticality markers (i.e., markers with higher ∆LL) were added to the concatenate (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Inter-domain gene transfers reduce the overall AB branch length when included in a concatenation.
source: These results suggest that inter-domain gene transfers reduce the overall AB branch length when included in a concatenation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' analyses of marker gene verticality and AB branch length.

claim: Mean root-to-tip distances were significantly positively correlated with ∆LL (R = 0.1397803, p=0.01506).
source: Mean root-to-tip distances were significantly positively correlated with ∆LL and between-domain split score (∆LL: R = 0.1397803, p=0.01506
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Mean root-to-tip distances were significantly positively correlated with between-domain split score (R = 0.1705415, p=0.002947).
source: split score: R = 0.1705415, p=0.002947; Figure 1—figure supplements 5 and 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 5 and 6.

claim: Vertically evolving genes evolve relatively slowly.
source: indicating that vertically evolving genes evolve relatively slowly (note that large values of ∆LL and split score denote low verticality).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the positive correlation between mean root-to-tip distances and ∆LL/split score.

claim: The longer AB branches of vertically evolving genes do not appear to result from a faster evolutionary rate for these genes.
source: Thus, the longer AB branches of vertically evolving genes do not appear to result from a faster evolutionary rate for these genes.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that vertically evolving genes evolve relatively slowly.

claim: The inclusion of genes that do not support the reciprocal monophyly of Archaea and Bacteria, or their constituent taxonomic ranks, in the universal concatenate explains the reduced estimated AB branch length.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the inclusion of genes that do not support the reciprocal monophyly of Archaea and Bacteria, or their constituent taxonomic ranks, in the universal concatenate explains the reduced estimated AB branch length.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' analyses of marker gene verticality and AB branch length.

claim: 54 markers recovered archaeal and bacterial monophyly after iterative phylogenetics and manual curation.
source: extracted homologous sequences from a representative sample of 350 archaeal and 350 bacterial genomes (Supplementary file 3), and performed iterative phylogenetics and manual curation to obtain a set of 54 markers that recovered archaeal and bacterial monophyly (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' phylogenetic analyses and manual curation.

claim: Prior to manual curation, non-ribosomal markers had a greater number of HGTs and cases of mixed paralogy.
source: Prior to manual curation, non-ribosomal markers had a greater number of HGTs (horizontal gene transfer) and cases of mixed paralogy.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' manual inspection of gene trees.

claim: For the original set of 95 unique COG families, 41 families were rejected based on the inferred ML trees either due to a large degree of HGT, paralogous gene families, or LBA.
source: In particular, for the original set of 95 unique COG families (see 'Phylogenetic analyses' in Materials and methods), we rejected 41 families based on the inferred ML trees either due to a large degree of HGT, paralogous gene families, or LBA (long branch attraction).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' manual inspection of gene trees.

claim: For the remaining 54 markers, the ML trees contained evidence of occasional recent HGT events.
source: For the remaining 54 markers, the ML trees contained evidence of occasional recent HGT events.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' manual inspection of gene trees.

claim: Strict monophyly was violated in 69% of the non-ribosomal and 29% of the ribosomal families.
source: Strict monophyly was violated in 69% of the non-ribosomal and 29% of the ribosomal families.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' manual inspection of gene trees.

claim: Manual curation of marker genes is important for deep phylogenetic analyses, particularly when using non-ribosomal markers.
source: These results imply that manual curation of marker genes is important for deep phylogenetic analyses, particularly when using non-ribosomal markers.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' observations of HGTs and mixed paralogy in non-ribosomal markers.

claim: Markers that better resolved established relationships within each domain also supported a longer AB branch length.
source: Comparison of within-domain split scores for these 54 markers (Supplementary file 4) indicated that markers that better resolved established relationships within each domain also supported a longer AB branch length (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The AB branch length inferred from a concatenation of the 54 marker genes increased moderately following pruning of recent HGTs, from 1.734 substitutions/site (non-pruned) to 1.945 substitutions/site after manual pruning.
source: Further, the AB branch length inferred from a concatenation of the 54 marker genes increased moderately following pruning of recent HGTs, from 1.734 substitutions/site (non-pruned) to 1.945 substitutions/site after manual pruning
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' phylogenetic analyses before and after manual pruning.

claim: Non-modeled inter-domain HGTs reduce the overall estimate of AB branch length when included in concatenations.
source: consistent with the hypothesis that non-modeled inter-domain HGTs reduce the overall estimate of AB branch length when included in concatenations.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the increase in AB branch length after pruning HGTs.

claim: There was no evidence that there was a longer AB branch associated with ribosomal markers than for other vertically evolving 'core' genes (mean AB branch length for ribosomal proteins 1.35 substitutions/site, mean for non-ribosomal 2.25 substitutions/site).
source: We found no evidence that there was a longer AB branch associated with ribosomal markers than for other vertically evolving 'core' genes (Figure 2B; mean AB branch length for ribosomal proteins 1.35 substitutions/site, mean for non-ribosomal 2.25 substitutions/site).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AB branch lengths from the ribosomal and non-ribosomal concatenates were similar overall, with some support for a longer AB branch length from vertically evolving non-ribosomal genes.
source: To investigate further, we compared AB branch lengths inferred from concatenates of the ribosomal and non-ribosomal subsets of the 54 ancient, vertically evolving genes (Table 1). AB branch lengths from the ribosomal and non-ribosomal concatenates were similar overall, with some support for a longer AB branch length from vertically evolving non-ribosomal genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The data do not support an accelerated evolutionary rate for ribosomal genes compared to other kinds of genes on the AB branch.
source: Thus, these data do not support an accelerated evolutionary rate for ribosomal genes compared to other kinds of genes on the AB branch.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' comparison of AB branch lengths from ribosomal and non-ribosomal concatenates.

claim: Slow-evolving sites support a relatively long inter-domain branch and less diversity within the domains.
source: Slow-evolving sites support a relatively long inter-domain branch and less diversity within the domains (i.e., shorter between-taxa branch lengths within domains).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Substitution saturation (overwriting of earlier changes) may reduce the relative length of the AB branch at fast-evolving sites and genes.
source: This suggests that substitution saturation (overwriting of earlier changes) may reduce the relative length of the AB branch at fast-evolving sites and genes.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that slow-evolving sites support a relatively long inter-domain branch.

claim: The proportion of inferred substitutions that occur along the AB branch differs between the slow-evolving and fast-evolving sites.
source: Notably, the proportion of inferred substitutions that occur along the AB branch differs between the slow-evolving and fast-evolving sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of site evolutionary rates.

claim: The relative AB branch length is longer for slow-evolving sites (1.2 substitutions/site, or ~2% of all inferred substitutions) compared to fast-evolving sites (2.6 substitutions/site, or ~0.04% of all inferred substitutions).
source: As would be expected, the total tree length measured in substitutions per site is shorter from the slow-evolving sites, but the relative AB branch length is longer (1.2 substitutions/site, or ~2% of all inferred substitutions, compared to 2.6 substitutions/site, or ~0.04% of all inferred substitutions for the fastest-evolving sites; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for absolute tree size comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of site evolutionary rates.

claim: Some ancient changes along the AB branch at fast-evolving sites have been overwritten by more recent events in evolution.
source: Since we would not expect the distribution of substitutions over the tree to differ between slow-evolving and fast-evolving sites, this result suggests that some ancient changes along the AB branch at fast-evolving sites have been overwritten by more recent events in evolution – that is, that substitutional saturation leads to an underestimate of the AB branch length
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the difference in relative AB branch length between slow- and fast-evolving sites.

claim: Substitutional saturation leads to an underestimate of the AB branch length.
source: that is, that substitutional saturation leads to an underestimate of the AB branch length (this is the case for both the expanded marker set and the 27 marker set; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the difference in relative AB branch length between slow- and fast-evolving sites.

claim: Failure to adequately model the site-specific features of sequence evolution leads to underestimation of genetic distance on deep branches.
source: Another factor that has been shown to lead to underestimation of genetic distance on deep branches is a failure to adequately model the site-specific features of sequence evolution (Lartillot and Philippe, 2004; Schrempf et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Amino acid preferences vary across the sites of a sequence alignment due to variation in the underlying functional constraints.
source: Amino acid preferences vary across the sites of a sequence alignment due to variation in the underlying functional constraints (Lartillot and Philippe, 2004; Quang et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At many alignment sites, only a subset of the 20 possible amino acids are tolerated by selection.
source: The consequence is that, at many alignment sites, only a subset of the 20 possible amino acids are tolerated by selection.
evidence: The claim is based on established principles of molecular evolution.

claim: Standard substitution models such as LG + G4 + F are site-homogeneous and approximate the composition of all sites using the average composition across the entire alignment.
source: Standard substitution models such as LG + G4 + F are site-homogeneous and approximate the composition of all sites using the average composition across the entire alignment.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of phylogenetic methods.

claim: Site-homogeneous models underestimate the rate of evolution at highly constrained sites because they do not account for the high number of multiple substitutions that occur at such sites.
source: Such models underestimate the rate of evolution at highly constrained sites because they do not account for the high number of multiple substitutions that occur at such sites.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of phylogenetic methods.

claim: Site-homogeneous models underestimate branch lengths when fit to site-heterogeneous data.
source: The effect is that site-homogeneous models underestimate branch lengths when fit to site-heterogeneous data.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of phylogenetic methods.

claim: Site-heterogeneous models have been developed that account for site-specific amino acid preferences, and these generally show improved fit to real protein sequence data.
source: Site-heterogeneous models have been developed that account for site-specific amino acid preferences, and these generally show improved fit to real protein sequence data (reviewed in Williams et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: The AB branch length inferred under the best-fit model, the site-heterogeneous LG + C60 + G4 + F model, was 2.52 substitutions/site, ~1.7-fold greater than the branch length inferred from the site-homogeneous LG + G4 + F model (1.45 substitutions/site).
source: The AB branch length inferred under the best-fit model, the site-heterogeneous LG + C60 + G4 + F model, was 2.52 substitutions/site, ~1.7-fold greater than the branch length inferred from the site-homogeneous LG + G4 + F model (1.45 substitutions/site).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' phylogenetic analyses using different substitution models.

claim: Substitution model fit has a major effect on the estimated length of the AB branch, with better-fitting models supporting a longer branch length.
source: Thus, substitution model fit has a major effect on the estimated length of the AB branch, with better-fitting models supporting a longer branch length (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' phylogenetic analyses using different substitution models.

claim: For the top 5% of genes by ∆LL score in the expanded marker set, the AB branch length is 1.2 under LG + G4 + F, but increases to 2.4 under the best-fitting LG + C60 + G4 + F model.
source: The same trends are evident when better-fitting site-heterogeneous models are used to analyze the expanded marker set: considering only the top 5% of genes by ∆LL score, the AB branch length is 1.2 under LG + G4 + F, but increases to 2.4 under the best-fitting LG + C60 + G4 + F model (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' phylogenetic analyses using different substitution models.

claim: Difficulties with modeling sequence evolution, either due to substitutional saturation or failure to model variation in site compositions, lead to an underestimation of the AB branch length.
source: Overall, these results indicate that difficulties with modeling sequence evolution, either due to substitutional saturation or failure to model variation in site compositions, lead to an underestimation of the AB branch length, both in published analyses and for the analyses of the new dataset presented here.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' analyses of site evolutionary rates and substitution models.

claim: As substitution models improve, we would expect estimates of the AB branch length to increase further.
source: As substitution models improve, we would therefore expect estimates of the AB branch length to increase further.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the authors' findings.

claim: The phylogeny inferred from the 27 most vertically evolving genes is consistent with recent single-domain trees inferred for Archaea and Bacteria independently.
source: The phylogeny of the primary domains of life inferred from the 27 most vertically evolving genes as inferred based on our ranking of markers and using the best-fitting LG + C60 + G4 + F model (Figure 4) is consistent with recent single-domain trees inferred for Archaea and Bacteria independently (Coleman et al., 2021; Dombrowski et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of the authors' phylogeny with previous studies.

claim: The deep relationships within Bacteria are poorly resolved, with the exception of the monophyly of Gracilicutes.
source: although the deep relationships within Bacteria are poorly resolved, with the exception of the monophyly of Gracilicutes (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 4.

claim: The authors' results are in good agreement with a recent estimate of the universal tree based on a different marker gene selection approach.
source: Our results are also in good agreement with a recent estimate of the universal tree based on a different marker gene selection approach (Martinez-Gutierrez and Aylward, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with a previous study.

claim: The authors recovered the DPANN, TACK, and Asgard Archaea as monophyletic groups.
source: Consistent with some recent studies (Dombrowski et al., 2020; Guy and Ettema, 2011; Raymann et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2017), we recovered the DPANN, TACK, and Asgard Archaea as monophyletic groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 4.

claim: The authors recovered a sister group relationship between candidate phyla radiation (CPR) and Chloroflexota.
source: Although the deep branches within Bacteria are poorly resolved, we recovered a sister group relationship between candidate phyla radiation (CPR) and Chloroflexota, consistent with recent reports (Taib et al., 2020; Coleman et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 4.

claim: The analysis placed the candidate phyla radiation (CPR) as a sister lineage to Chloroflexi (Chloroflexota) rather than as a deep-branching bacterial superphylum.
source: In particular, our analysis placed the candidate phyla radiation (CPR) (Brown et al., 2015) as a sister lineage to Chloroflexi (Chloroflexota) rather than as a deep-branching bacterial superphylum.
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree inferred from the 27 marker genes.

claim: The finding that CPR is sister to Chloroflexota is consistent with recent analyses that have recovered CPR within the Terrabacteria.
source: While this contrasts with initial trees suggesting that CPR may represent an early diverging sister lineage of all other Bacteria (Brown et al., 2015; Castelle and Banfield, 2018; Hug et al., 2016), our finding is consistent with recent analyses that have instead recovered CPR within the Terrabacteria (Coleman et al., 2021; Martinez-Gutierrez and Aylward, 2021; Taib et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous studies.

claim: The deep-branching position of CPR in some trees may be a result of long branch attraction.
source: Together, these analyses suggest that the deep-branching position of CPR in some trees may be a result of long branch attraction, a possibility that has been raised previously (Hug et al., 2016; Méheust et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' phylogenetic results and previous studies.

claim: The deep branches of the archaeal subtree are generally well-resolved and recover DPANN (51% bootstrap support), Asgards (100% bootstrap support), and TACK Archaea (75% bootstrap support) as monophyletic clades.
source: The deep branches of the archaeal subtree are generally well-resolved and recover DPANN (51% bootstrap support), Asgards (100% bootstrap support), and TACK Archaea (75% bootstrap support) as monophyletic clades in agreement with a range of previous studies (Guy and Ettema, 2011; Dombrowski et al., 2020; Guy and Ettema, 2011; Raymann et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree inferred from the 27 marker genes.

claim: The authors find support for the placement of Methanonatronarchaeia distant to Halobacteria as one of the earliest branches of the Methanotecta.
source: We also find support for the placement of Methanonatronarchaeia (Sorokin et al., 2017) distant to Halobacteria as one of the earliest branches of the Methanotecta (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 3) in agreement with recent analyses, suggesting that their initial placement with Halobacteria (Sorokin et al., 2017) may be an artifact of compositional attraction (Aouad et al., 2019; Dombrowski et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2021; Martijn et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree inferred from the 27 marker genes.

claim: The authors obtained moderate (92%) bootstrap support for the branching of some Euryarchaeota with the TACK + Asgard clade.
source: We obtained moderate (92%) bootstrap support for the branching of some Euryarchaeota with the TACK + Asgard clade: the Hadesarchaea + Persephonarchaea were resolved as the sister group to TACK + Asgards with moderate (92%) support, with this entire lineage branching sister to a strongly supported (100%) clade comprising Theionarchaea, Methanofastidiosa, and Thermococcales.
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree inferred from the 27 marker genes.

claim: The position of Hadesarchaea, Persephonarchaea, Theionarchaea, Methanofastidiosa, and Thermococcales was sensitive to the marker gene set used.
source: However, the position of these lineages was sensitive to the marker gene set used.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of phylogenies inferred from different marker gene sets.

claim: In the 25-gene analysis, Hadesarchaea, Persephonarchaea, Theionarchaea, Methanofastidiosa, and Thermococcales branched with Methanomada with high support (98%).
source: As part of a robustness test, we also inferred an additional tree from a 25-gene subset, excluding two genes that have complex evolutionary histories in Archaea (Narrowe et al., 2018; Figure 4—figure supplement 3). In this analysis, these Archaea instead branched with Methanomada with high support (98%), highlighting the difficulty of placing these lineages in the archaeal tree.
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree inferred from the 25 marker genes.

claim: Euryarchaeotal paraphyly has been previously reported.
source: Euryarchaeotal paraphyly has been previously reported (Adam et al., 2017; Raymann et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2017; Aouad et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The extent of the observed euryarchaeotal paraphyly and the lineages involved has varied among analyses.
source: though the extent of the observed paraphyly and the lineages involved has varied among analyses.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of results from different studies.

claim: A basal placement of DPANN within Archaea is sometimes viewed with suspicion because DPANN genomes are reduced and appear to be fast-evolving, properties that may cause LBA artifacts.
source: A basal placement of DPANN within Archaea is sometimes viewed with suspicion (Aouad et al., 2018) because DPANN genomes are reduced and appear to be fast-evolving, properties that may cause LBA artifacts (Dombrowski et al., 2019) when analyses include Bacteria.
evidence: The claim is based on previous studies and established knowledge of phylogenetic artifacts.

claim: The early divergence of DPANN from the archaeal branch has received support from a number of recent studies.
source: However, in contrast to CPR, with which DPANN share certain ecological and genomic similarities (e.g., host dependency, small genomes, limited metabolic potential), the early divergence of DPANN from the archaeal branch has received support from a number of recent studies (Baker et al., 2020; Beam et al., 2020; Dombrowski et al., 2020; Rinke et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2017; Zaremba-Niedzwiedzka et al., 2017; Aouad et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The inclusion of certain lineages within DPANN remains controversial.
source: though the inclusion of certain lineages within this radiation remains controversial (Aouad et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The placement of the root within DPANN is uncertain.
source: and the placement of the root is uncertain (Dombrowski et al., 2020; Aouad et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The phylogenetic diversity of the archaeal and bacterial domains, measured as substitutions per site in the consensus set of vertically evolving marker genes, appears to be similar.
source: A broader observation from our analysis is that the phylogenetic diversity of the archaeal and bacterial domains, measured as substitutions per site in this consensus set of vertically evolving marker genes, appears to be similar (Figure 3A; the mean root-to-tip distance for archaea: 2.38, for bacteria: 2.41; the range of root-to-tip distances for archaea: 1.79–3.01, for bacteria: 1.70–3.17).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of root-to-tip distances.

claim: Considering only the slowest-evolving category of sites, branch lengths within Archaea are actually longer than within Bacteria.
source: Considering only the slowest-evolving category of sites, branch lengths within Archaea are actually longer than within Bacteria (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The choice of marker genes has a profound impact on the apparent phylogenetic diversity of certain prokaryotic groups.
source: Our analyses and a number of previous studies (Hug et al., 2016; Parks et al., 2018; Petitjean et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2019) indicate that the choice of marker genes has a profound impact on the apparent phylogenetic diversity of certain prokaryotic groups; for instance, in the proportion of bacterial diversity composed of CPR (Hug et al., 2016; Parks et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analyses and citations to previous studies.

claim: Slow- and fast-evolving sites from the same set of marker genes support different tree shapes and branch lengths.
source: Our results demonstrate that slow- and fast-evolving sites from the same set of marker genes support different tree shapes and branch lengths
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of site evolutionary rates.

claim: Between-dataset differences in phylogenetic diversity are due, at least in part, to evolutionary rate variation within and between marker genes.
source: it therefore seems possible that between-dataset differences are due, at least in part, to evolutionary rate variation within and between marker genes.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' findings.

claim: Estimates of the ages of the deepest branches, and their lengths in geological time, remain highly uncertain.
source: While a consensus may be emerging on the topology of the universal tree, estimates of the ages of the deepest branches, and their lengths in geological time, remain highly uncertain.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' molecular clock analyses and the limitations of current methods.

claim: The fossil record of early life is incomplete and difficult to interpret.
source: The fossil record of early life is incomplete and difficult to interpret (Wacey, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Molecular clock methods provide a means of combining the abundant genetic data available for modern organisms with the limited fossil record to improve our understanding of early evolution.
source: and in this context molecular clock methods provide a means of combining the abundant genetic data available for modern organisms with the limited fossil record to improve our understanding of early evolution (Betts et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The 381-gene dataset was suggested to be useful for inferring deep divergence times because age estimates of LUCA from this dataset using a strict molecular clock were in agreement with the geological record.
source: The 381-gene dataset was suggested to be (Zhu et al., 2019) useful for inferring deep divergence times because age estimates of LUCA (last universal common ancestor) from this dataset using a strict molecular clock were in agreement with the geological record: a root (LUCA) age of 3.6–4.2 Ga was inferred from the entire 381-gene dataset, consistent with the earliest fossil evidence for life (Betts et al., 2018; Sugitani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is a statement about a previous study.

claim: Analysis of ribosomal markers alone supported a root age of ~7 Ga, which might be considered implausible because it is older than the age of the Earth and Solar System.
source: By contrast, analysis of ribosomal markers alone (Zhu et al., 2019) supported a root age of ~7 Ga, which might be considered implausible because it is older than the age of the Earth and Solar System (with the moon-forming impact occurring ~4.52 Ga; Barboni et al., 2017; Hanan and Tilton, 1987).
evidence: The claim is a statement about a previous study and its implications.

claim: The published molecular clock analyses made use of concatenation-based branch lengths in which topological disagreement among sites is not modeled and are likely to be affected by the impact of nonvertical marker genes and substitutional saturation on branch length estimation.
source: The published molecular clock analyses (Zhu et al., 2019) made use of concatenation-based branch lengths in which topological disagreement among sites is not modeled and are likely to be affected by the impact of nonvertical marker genes and substitutional saturation on branch length estimation discussed above.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' analyses of the expanded marker set.

claim: Divergence time inference using the same method on the 5% most-vertical subset of the expanded marker set resulted in age estimates for LUCA that exceed the age of the Earth, 5.6–6.15 Ga.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, divergence time inference using the same method on the 5% most-vertical subset of the expanded marker set (as determined by ∆LL; this set of 20 genes includes only one ribosomal protein, see Supplementary file 5a) resulted in age estimates for LUCA that exceed the age of the Earth, 5.6–6.15 Ga (Figure 5), approaching the age inferred from the ribosomal genes (7.46–8.03 Ga).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: The apparent agreement between the fossil record and divergence times estimated from the expanded gene set may be due, at least in part, to the shortening of the AB branch due to phylogenetic incongruence among marker genes.
source: These results (Figure 5) suggest that the apparent agreement between the fossil record and divergence times estimated from the expanded gene set may be due, at least in part, to the shortening of the AB branch due to phylogenetic incongruence among marker genes.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: The age of LUCA was estimated using a strict clock with a single calibration constraining the split between Cyanobacteria and Melainabacteria in the original analyses.
source: In the original analyses, the age of LUCA was estimated using a strict clock with a single calibration constraining the split between Cyanobacteria and Melainabacteria derived from estimates of the Great Oxidation Event and a secondary estimate of the age of cyanobacteria derived from an independent analysis (Shih et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is a description of the methods used in a previous study.

claim: The combination of a strict clock and only two calibrations is not sufficient to capture the variation in evolutionary rate over deep timescales.
source: The combination of a strict clock and only two calibrations is not sufficient to capture the variation in evolutionary rate over deep timescales (Drummond et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: All of the additional calibrations used by the authors were minimum age calibrations with the exception of the root.
source: Unfortunately, all of these were minimum age calibrations with the exception of the root (for which the moon-forming impact 4.52 Ga [Kleine et al., 2005] provides a reasonable maximum) due to the difficulty of establishing uncontroversial maximum ages for microbial clades.
evidence: The claim is a description of the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: Maximum age constraints are essential to inform faster rates of evolution.
source: Maximum age constraints are essential to inform faster rates of evolution because, in combination with more abundant minimum age constraints, they imply that a given number of substitutions must have accumulated in at most a certain interval of time.
evidence: The claim is based on established principles of molecular clock methods.

claim: In the absence of other maximum age constraints, the only lower bound on the rate of molecular evolution is provided by the maximum age constraint on the root (LUCA).
source: In the absence of other maximum age constraints, the only lower bound on the rate of molecular evolution is provided by the maximum age constraint on the root (LUCA).
evidence: The claim is based on established principles of molecular clock methods.

claim: The age of LUCA inferred from the 27-gene dataset was unrealistically old, falling close to the maximum age constraint in all analyses even when the maximum was set to the age of the known universe (13.7 Ga).
source: These new analyses indicated that even with additional minimum age calibrations the age of LUCA inferred from the 27-gene dataset was unrealistically old, falling close to the maximum age constraint in all analyses even when the maximum was set to the age of the known universe (13.7 Ga; Aghanim, 2018; Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: The mean rate of molecular evolution inferred from the 27-gene dataset is low (mean = 0.21, 95% credibility interval = 0.19–0.22 subs. site–1 Ga–1).
source: Inspection of the inferred rates of molecular evolution across the tree (Figure 5B) provides some insight into these results: the mean rate is low (mean = 0.21, 95% credibility interval = 0.19–0.22 subs. site–1 Ga–1)
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: Long branches, in the absence of other information, are interpreted as evidence of a long period of geological time.
source: so that long branches (such as the AB stem), in the absence of other information, are interpreted as evidence of a long period of geological time.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: The low rates of molecular evolution inferred from the 27-gene dataset likely result both from the limited number of calibrations and, in particular, the lack of maximum age constraints.
source: These low rates likely result both from the limited number of calibrations and, in particular, the lack of maximum age constraints.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: The LUCA to LACA branch has a rate 10-fold greater than the average (mean = 2.51, 95% HPD = 1.6–3.5 subs. site–1 Ga–1).
source: An interesting outlier among inferred rates is the LUCA to LACA (last archaeal common ancestor) branch, which has a rate 10-fold greater than the average (mean = 2.51, 95% HPD (highest posterior density) = 1.6–3.5 subs. site–1 Ga–1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: Calibrations within Bacteria imply that LBCA cannot be younger than 3.225 Ga.
source: The reason is that calibrations within Bacteria imply that LBCA (last bacterial common ancestor) cannot be younger than 3.225 Ga (Manzimnyama Banded Ironstone Formation provides evidence of cyanobacterial oxygenation; Satkoski et al., 2015, Supplementary file 5b)
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' molecular clock analyses and fossil calibrations.

claim: With a 4.52 Ga maximum, the LUCA to LBCA branch cannot be longer than 1.295 Ga.
source: as a result, with a 4.52 Ga maximum, the LUCA to LBCA branch cannot be longer than 1.295 Ga.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: The early branches of the archaeal tree are poorly constrained by fossil evidence.
source: By contrast, the early branches of the archaeal tree are poorly constrained by fossil evidence.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' molecular clock analyses and the limited availability of fossil calibrations for Archaea.

claim: Analysis without the 3.225 Ga constraint resulted in overlapping age estimates for LBCA (4.47–3.53 Ga) and LACA (4.37–3.44 Ga).
source: Analysis without the 3.225 Ga constraint resulted in overlapping age estimates for LBCA (4.47–3.53 Ga) and LACA (4.37–3.44 Ga).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: Analysis of the archaeal and bacterial subtrees independently resulted in LBCA and LACA ages that abut the maximum root age (LBCA: 4.52–4.38 Ga; LACA: 4.52–4.14 Ga).
source: Finally, analysis of the archaeal and bacterial subtrees independently (i.e., without the AB branch, rooted on LACA and LBCA, respectively) resulted in LBCA and LACA ages that abut the maximum root age (LBCA: 4.52–4.38 Ga; LACA: 4.52–4.14 Ga).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: Under the analysis conditions used, the inferred age of the root is strongly influenced by the prior assumptions about the maximum age of the root.
source: This analysis demonstrates that, under these analysis conditions, the inferred age of the root (whether corresponding to LUCA, LACA, or LBCA) is strongly influenced by the prior assumptions about the maximum age of the root.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: The agreement between fossils and age estimates from the expanded gene set appears to result from the impact of phylogenetic incongruence on branch length estimates.
source: In sum, the agreement between fossils and age estimates from the expanded gene set appears to result from the impact of phylogenetic incongruence on branch length estimates.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: The sequence data only contain limited information about the age of the root, with posterior estimates driven by the prior assumptions about the maximum age of the root.
source: Under more flexible modeling assumptions, the limitations of current clock methods for estimating the age of LUCA become manifest: the sequence data only contain limited information about the age of the root, with posterior estimates driven by the prior assumptions about the maximum age of the root.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: More calibrations, particularly maximum age constraints and calibrations within Archaea, are essential to refine the current estimates of the age of LUCA.
source: This analysis implies several possible ways to improve age estimates of deep branches in future analyses. More calibrations, particularly maximum age constraints and calibrations within Archaea, are essential to refine the current estimates.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: Constraints from other sources such as donor-recipient age constraints inferred from HGTs, or clock models that capture biological opinion about rate shifts in early evolution, may be particularly valuable for improving age estimates of deep branches.
source: Given the difficulties in establishing maximum ages for archaeal and bacterial clades, constraints from other sources such as donor-recipient age constraints inferred from HGTs (Davín et al., 2018; Fournier et al., 2021; Szöllősi et al., 2021; Wolfe and Fournier, 2018), or clock models that capture biological opinion about rate shifts in early evolution, may be particularly valuable.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: The choice of markers and the fit of the substitution model are both important for inference of deep phylogeny from concatenations.
source: Our analysis of a range of published marker gene datasets (Petitjean et al., 2014; Spang et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2019) indicates that the choice of markers and the fit of the substitution model are both important for inference of deep phylogeny from concatenations, in agreement with an existing body of literature (reviewed in Kapli et al., 2021; Kapli et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' analyses and citations to previous studies.

claim: The authors established a set of 27 vertically evolving marker gene families and found no evidence that ribosomal genes overestimate stem length.
source: We established a set of 27 vertically evolving marker gene families and found no evidence that ribosomal genes overestimate stem length
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' analyses.

claim: Ribosomal proteins are useful markers for deep phylogeny because they appear to be transferred less frequently than other genes.
source: since they appear to be transferred less frequently than other genes, our analysis affirms that ribosomal proteins are useful markers for deep phylogeny.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' analyses.

claim: High-verticality markers, regardless of functional category, supported a longer AB branch length.
source: In general, high-verticality markers, regardless of functional category, supported a longer AB branch length.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' analyses.

claim: The authors' phylogeny was consistent with recent work on early prokaryotic evolution, resolving the major clades within Archaea and nesting the CPR within Terrabacteria.
source: Furthermore, our phylogeny was consistent with recent work on early prokaryotic evolution, resolving the major clades within Archaea and nesting the CPR within Terrabacteria.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The authors' analyses suggested that both the true AB branch length and the phylogenetic diversity of Archaea may be underestimated by even the best current models.
source: Notably, our analyses suggested that both the true AB branch length (Figure 6A) and the phylogenetic diversity of Archaea may be underestimated by even the best current models
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' analyses.

claim: The finding that both the true AB branch length and the phylogenetic diversity of Archaea may be underestimated is consistent with a root for the tree of life between the two prokaryotic domains.
source: a finding that is consistent with a root for the tree of life between the two prokaryotic domains.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' findings.

claim: The long AB branch length inferred from vertically evolving genes is consistent with the hypothesis that rates of molecular evolution may have been higher early in life's history than more recently.
source: Taken together with fossil evidence for crown-group Bacteria ~3.2 Ga (Betts et al., 2018), the long AB branch length inferred from vertically evolving genes is consistent with the hypothesis that rates of molecular evolution may have been higher early in life's history than more recently (Lopez et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' findings and fossil evidence.

claim: The inferred rates of molecular evolution are uncertain and contingent on limited fossil evidence and the assumptions of the molecular clock model.
source: although the inferred rates are uncertain and contingent on limited fossil evidence and the assumptions of the molecular clock model.
evidence: The claim is a caveat based on the authors' molecular clock analyses.

claim: Core genes comprise only a small proportion of prokaryotic genomes and have sometimes been viewed as outliers in the sense that they are unusually vertical among prokaryotic gene families.
source: Phylogenies inferred from 'core' genes involved in translation and other conserved cellular processes have provided one of the few available windows into the earliest period of archaeal and bacterial evolution. However, core genes comprise only a small proportion of prokaryotic genomes and have sometimes been viewed as outliers (Zhu et al., 2019) in the sense that they are unusually vertical among prokaryotic gene families.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' discussion and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Core genes are among the few prokaryotic gene families amenable to concatenation methods.
source: This means that they are among the few prokaryotic gene families amenable to concatenation methods, which are useful for pooling signal from individual weakly resolved gene trees but which make the assumption that all sites evolve on the same underlying tree.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of phylogenetic methods.

claim: If other gene families are included in concatenations, the results can be difficult to predict because differences in topology across sites are not modeled.
source: If other gene families are included in concatenations, the results can be difficult to predict because differences in topology across sites are not modeled.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of phylogenetic methods.

claim: The authors' analyses of the 381-gene expanded set suggest that phylogenetic incongruence can lead to underestimation of the evolutionary distance between Archaea and Bacteria.
source: Our analyses of the 381-gene expanded set suggest that this incongruence can lead to underestimation of the evolutionary distance between Archaea and Bacteria, in the sense of the branch length separating the archaeal and bacterial domains.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the authors' analyses.

claim: In a phenetic sense of overall genome similarity, extensive HGT will increase the evolutionary proximity of the domains so that Archaea and Bacteria may become intermixed at the single-gene level.
source: We note that alternative conceptions of evolutionary distance are possible; for example, in a phenetic sense of overall genome similarity, extensive HGT will increase the evolutionary proximity (Zhu et al., 2019) of the domains so that Archaea and Bacteria may become intermixed at the single-gene level.
evidence: The claim is a discussion of alternative interpretations of evolutionary distance.

claim: It is unsatisfactory to base our view of early evolution on a relatively small set of genes that appear to experience selective pressures rather distinct from the forces at play more broadly in prokaryotic genome evolution.
source: At the same time, it is clearly unsatisfactory to base our view of early evolution on a relatively small set of genes that appear to experience selective pressures rather distinct from the forces at play more broadly in prokaryotic genome evolution.
evidence: The claim is a discussion of the limitations of using core genes for phylogenetic inference.

claim: Exploring the evolutionary signal in more of the genome than hitherto is a worthwhile endeavor.
source: Exploring the evolutionary signal in more of the genome than hitherto is clearly a worthwhile endeavor.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the authors' discussion.

claim: New methods, including more realistic models of gene duplication, transfer and loss, and extensions to supertree methods to model paralogy and gene transfer, promise to enable genome-wide inference of prokaryotic history and evolutionary processes.
source: New methods, including more realistic models of gene duplication, transfer and loss (Morel et al., 2021; Szöllõsi et al., 2013), and extensions to supertree methods to model paralogy (Zhang et al., 2020) and gene transfer, promise to enable genome-wide inference of prokaryotic history and evolutionary processes using methods that can account for the varying evolutionary histories of individual gene families.
evidence: The claim is a discussion of future directions for phylogenetic methods.
